items.prompt: The web team adds a field to a response shape for a homepage banner. That night, the mobile app crashes and a partner integration stops receiving orders. Neither team touched mobile or partner code. What does this tell you?
choices: Mobile and the partner both shipped buggy code around the same time, by coincidence
Web, mobile, and the partner were sharing one endpoint with no boundary marking where one consumer's concerns ended and another's began
The database itself is unreliable and needs to be replaced
This can only happen if the web team wrote sloppy code
items.explanation: A change made for one consumer's benefit leaking into another consumer's failure is the signature symptom of a missing service boundary — all three consumers were reaching into the same undifferentiated surface, so a change anywhere was effectively a change to everyone's contract.
items.reference:
🌐 Web changes a field
📱 Mobile crashes — unrelated code
🤝 Partner orders stop — unrelated code

Why: one shared surface means one consumer's change is everyone's risk.

items.prompt: A single `/products/:id` endpoint serves a web app, a mobile app, and a partner integration. The mobile team asks: 'can we get a smaller response so we don't burn cellular data?' Why is this request, on its own, evidence of a missing boundary rather than just a normal feature request?
choices: It isn't evidence of anything — this is a completely normal request
Because satisfying it (shrinking the shared response) would risk breaking web and the partner, who are relying on that same shared shape for different reasons
Because mobile apps should never call HTTP APIs
Because cellular data usage is not a backend team's concern
items.explanation: The request itself is reasonable, but fulfilling it on a shared endpoint means every change has to satisfy three consumers with different, sometimes conflicting needs — the tell-tale sign that a boundary (like a per-consumer BFF) is missing, not that anyone asked for something unreasonable.
items.reference:
🌐 Web changes a field
📱 Mobile crashes — unrelated code
🤝 Partner orders stop — unrelated code

Why: one shared surface means one consumer's change is everyone's risk.

items.prompt: What does a Backend for Frontend (BFF) do that a single shared backend endpoint does not?
choices: It replaces the database entirely
It gives each consumer type its own thin backend, shaped for that consumer's needs, in front of shared internal services
It removes the need for any backend at all
It forces every consumer to use the exact same response shape
items.explanation: A BFF is a thin, consumer-specific layer sitting in front of shared services — it lets web, mobile, and a partner each get a differently-shaped response without any of them touching the others' logic.
items.reference:
Web BFF

rich shape

Mobile BFF

lean shape

Partner API

frozen shape

Why: each BFF calls the same core service but shapes the response for exactly its own consumer.

items.prompt: In a BFF architecture, if the web BFF's response shape changes, what happens to the mobile BFF?
choices: It automatically adopts the same change
Nothing, as long as the underlying shared core service didn't change — each BFF shapes its own response independently
It stops working until manually redeployed
BFFs cannot exist independently of each other
items.explanation: That's the entire point of splitting shaping logic into separate BFFs — a change scoped to one consumer's BFF file has no path to affect another consumer's BFF file, as long as the shared core service underneath both stays the same.
items.reference:
Web BFF

rich shape

Mobile BFF

lean shape

Partner API

frozen shape

Why: each BFF calls the same core service but shapes the response for exactly its own consumer.

items.prompt: What's the main difference between an API gateway and a BFF?
choices: There is no difference, they're the same pattern under two names
A gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limits, routing) for everyone behind it; a BFF shapes data per consumer type
A gateway is only for mobile apps, a BFF is only for web apps
A BFF replaces the need for a database, a gateway does not
items.explanation: A gateway is about one control point for cross-cutting concerns (who's allowed in, how many requests per minute, routing). A BFF is about shaping a response for one consumer type. They solve different problems and often coexist — the gateway in front, BFFs behind it.
items.reference:
PatternSolves
BFFPer-consumer response shape
GatewayAuth, rate limits, routing — one control point

Why: they address different concerns and are often used together, gateway in front of BFFs.

items.prompt: A team wants a single place to enforce 'no more than 100 requests per minute per API key' across web, mobile, and partner traffic. Which pattern most directly addresses this?
choices: A BFF per consumer, since rate limits are consumer-specific
An API gateway, since rate limiting is a cross-cutting concern best enforced at one control point
A micro-frontend, since this is a UI concern
This cannot be solved with any of the patterns in this unit
items.explanation: Rate limiting across all traffic, regardless of which BFF or backend it eventually reaches, is exactly the kind of cross-cutting concern an API gateway centralizes — enforcing it separately inside every BFF would duplicate the same logic three times.
items.reference:
PatternSolves
BFFPer-consumer response shape
GatewayAuth, rate limits, routing — one control point

Why: they address different concerns and are often used together, gateway in front of BFFs.

items.prompt: Which of these is a breaking change to an API contract?
choices: Adding a new optional field that old consumers can ignore
Adding a brand new endpoint that nobody was calling before
Renaming an existing field that consumers currently read
Loosening a validation rule so more requests are accepted
items.explanation: Renaming or removing a field a consumer currently reads breaks that consumer immediately — it changes something they already rely on, unlike adding new optional fields or endpoints, which existing consumers can simply ignore.
items.reference:
Non-breaking

add optional field, add endpoint, loosen validation

Breaking

rename/remove a field, change a type, tighten validation

items.prompt: A team tightens a validation rule so that a field which used to accept any string must now match a stricter format. From an existing consumer's point of view, is this breaking or non-breaking?
choices: Non-breaking — validation changes never affect consumers
Breaking — requests that used to be accepted may now be rejected
It depends only on which programming language the backend uses
Breaking only if the consumer is a partner, never if it's internal
items.explanation: Tightening validation can reject requests that previously succeeded, which is exactly the definition of a breaking change from the consumer's point of view — whether the consumer is internal or external doesn't change whether it's breaking, only how painful it is to recover from.
items.reference:
Non-breaking

add optional field, add endpoint, loosen validation

Breaking

rename/remove a field, change a type, tighten validation

items.prompt: What is a micro-frontend, in one sentence?
choices: A frontend written in fewer than 100 lines of code
A UI surface built, owned, and deployed independently by the team responsible for it, then composed with other surfaces
A mobile-only version of a web app
A frontend framework with a smaller bundle size than React
items.explanation: A micro-frontend carries the same boundary idea from the backend up to the UI layer — different UI surfaces owned and deployed independently, then composed together, rather than one team owning every surface in one codebase.
items.reference:
Backend boundary: BFF per consumer
UI boundary: micro-frontend per owning team

Why: the same coupling problem shows up in the UI layer once multiple teams own multiple surfaces.

items.prompt: A single frontend codebase now serves the web storefront, a partner-embeddable widget, and an internal admin tool — all owned by one team. What pressure does this create, similar to Bramble's original shared backend endpoint?
choices: None — frontends don't experience this kind of pressure
A change made for one UI surface risks affecting the others, the same combinatorial coupling cost as one shared backend endpoint serving multiple consumers
This is actually the recommended long-term architecture with no downsides
This only matters if the team uses more than one programming language
items.explanation: One frontend codebase serving multiple independent UI surfaces has the same shape as one shared backend endpoint serving multiple consumers — a change for one surface's benefit can leak into another's failure, which is exactly the pressure micro-frontends are meant to relieve.
items.reference:
Backend boundary: BFF per consumer
UI boundary: micro-frontend per owning team

Why: the same coupling problem shows up in the UI layer once multiple teams own multiple surfaces.

items.prompt: A BFF or API gateway isolates consumers from each other's changes. What's the trade-off for that isolation?
choices: There is no trade-off — boundaries are strictly free once built
Another service to build, deploy, version, and keep someone on call for
It always makes response times faster with no other cost
It removes the need for any testing
items.explanation: Every boundary pattern in this unit trades coupling for coordination and operational cost — a BFF, gateway, or micro-frontend is one more thing to build, deploy, and staff, not a free win.
items.reference: Boundaries aren't free: each one is a service to run, deploy, and be on call for.

items.prompt: A small internal admin tool has exactly one consumer and no external partners. Does it need a BFF and an API gateway?
choices: Yes — every backend should always have both by default
No — with only one real consumer there's nothing to isolate from anything else, so the boundary's coordination cost buys nothing
Only the gateway, never the BFF, regardless of the situation
Only if the tool is written in a compiled language
items.explanation: Boundaries exist to isolate consumers with diverging needs from each other. With a single consumer there's no second party to protect from a shared change, so adding a BFF or gateway here is pure coordination cost with nothing bought in return.
items.reference: Boundaries aren't free: each one is a service to run, deploy, and be on call for.

items.prompt: What is a 'service boundary,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A firewall rule between two data centers
A line around a piece of a system where something stable is promised to dependents, and everything inside is free to change without asking permission
The maximum number of consumers a backend is allowed to have
A synonym for 'microservice'
items.explanation: A service boundary is about a promise, not a technology: what's outside the line can rely on a stable contract, and what's inside the line can change freely as long as that contract holds.
items.reference: A boundary = a promise to whoever's outside it + freedom to change whatever's inside it.

items.prompt: Bramble's original single `/products/:id` endpoint had no boundary at all. What specifically was missing?
choices: A load balancer in front of the endpoint
Any line marking where the backend's freely-changeable internals ended and a promise made to an outside consumer began
A caching layer
A second copy of the database
items.explanation: The missing piece wasn't infrastructure like a load balancer or cache — it was a boundary marking which parts of the response were an internal implementation detail versus a promise a consumer could rely on.
items.reference: A boundary = a promise to whoever's outside it + freedom to change whatever's inside it.

items.prompt: Bramble's team tried fixing the shared-endpoint problem with an 'ignore unknown fields' convention plus a handful of consumer-specific optional fields. Why did the endpoint's complexity keep climbing instead of leveling off?
choices: Because the team used the wrong programming language
Because each consumer's assumptions still had to coexist in one file, one review process, and one deploy — the number of combinations to reason about grows faster than the number of consumers
Because 'ignore unknown fields' is technically impossible to implement
It didn't actually keep climbing — this was a one-time cost
items.explanation: With consumer-specific logic living inside one shared endpoint, the endpoint has to reason about every combination of which fields are present for which consumer — that's closer to combinatorial growth than linear growth as consumers are added, which is why patching the endpoint kept getting harder, not easier.
items.reference:
1 consumer → 1 shape. 3 consumers with per-consumer fields → every combination of which fields are present, not just 3 shapes.

Why: complexity that isn't drawn into a boundary compounds instead of staying separate.

items.prompt: The chart in L2 shows conditional branches growing from 1 (one consumer) to roughly 16 (four consumers) inside one shared endpoint. What does that growth curve tell you about patching a shared endpoint as more consumers are added?
choices: That patching scales fine indefinitely, since each new consumer only adds a small amount of code
That the cost of patching grows faster than the number of consumers, because each addition has to coexist with every prior consumer's assumptions
That the chart is only about performance, not maintainability
That this only applies if all consumers are external partners
items.explanation: The growth isn't linear — it's closer to combinatorial, because each new consumer's needs have to be reconciled against every existing consumer's needs inside the same file. That's the concrete reason 'just add a conditional' stops being a viable long-term fix.
items.reference:
1 consumer → 1 shape. 3 consumers with per-consumer fields → every combination of which fields are present, not just 3 shapes.

Why: complexity that isn't drawn into a boundary compounds instead of staying separate.

items.prompt: In a BFF architecture, the web BFF and the mobile BFF both call the same shared core service. If the web BFF adds a new field to its own response, what happens to the mobile BFF's response?
choices: The mobile BFF automatically gains the same field
Nothing changes in the mobile BFF's response, because the new field only exists inside the web BFF's own shaping logic
The core service must be redeployed for mobile to catch up
The mobile app crashes the same way it did before BFFs were introduced
items.explanation: Each BFF shapes its own response independently from the shared core data — a field added inside one BFF's shaping code has no path to reach another BFF's response, which is the entire point of the pattern.
items.reference:
Web BFF→Core service←Mobile BFF

Why: each BFF owns its own shaping logic; only the core service is genuinely shared.

items.prompt: A team removes a field directly from the shared core service that both the web BFF and mobile BFF read. Does the BFF pattern protect either BFF from this specific change?
choices: Yes, completely — BFFs are immune to any change in the core service
No — the BFF pattern isolates consumer-specific shaping from each other, but every BFF still depends directly on the core service's actual shape
Only the web BFF is protected, never the mobile BFF
This scenario is impossible in a BFF architecture
items.explanation: BFFs isolate consumers from each other's consumer-specific fields, not from changes to the shared core service underneath all of them. A field removed from the core service can still break every BFF that reads it — that's why the core service's own contract needs its own discipline (see L3's versioning and contract tests).
items.reference:
Web BFF→Core service←Mobile BFF

Why: each BFF owns its own shaping logic; only the core service is genuinely shared.

items.prompt: A team wants strong isolation between the host page and an embedded partner widget — a bad deploy on the partner's side should never crash the host page. Which micro-frontend integration style gives the strongest isolation?
choices: Build-time npm package import
Runtime iframe embedding
Server-side composition at the edge
There is no integration style that provides isolation
items.explanation: An iframe runs in its own isolated browsing context — a crash or script error inside it can't directly bring down the host page, at the cost of awkward cross-frame styling and communication. Build-time imports and module federation share more of the runtime, trading isolation for tighter integration.
items.reference:
StyleTrade-off
Build-timeSimple, but every consumer redeploys to update
IframeStrong isolation, awkward cross-frame communication
Module federationIndependent deploys, shared runtime risk
Server-side/edgeNo client coordination, extra server hop

items.prompt: A team wants each UI surface's team to deploy independently and often, while still sharing the same runtime and some common libraries to avoid duplicating everything. Which integration style fits best?
choices: Build-time npm package import, since it's the simplest option
Module federation, since it allows independently deployed bundles to be composed at runtime while sharing the runtime environment
An iframe, since isolation is always the top priority
None of these styles support independent deploys
items.explanation: Module federation is specifically designed for independently deployed bundles that get loaded and composed together at runtime, sharing the host runtime — at the cost that a badly-behaved remote can still affect the host, unlike the stronger isolation an iframe provides.
items.reference:
StyleTrade-off
Build-timeSimple, but every consumer redeploys to update
IframeStrong isolation, awkward cross-frame communication
Module federationIndependent deploys, shared runtime risk
Server-side/edgeNo client coordination, extra server hop

items.prompt: What should decide where a service boundary line is drawn, according to L2?
choices: The org chart — boundaries should always mirror team reporting lines exactly
Which technology stack a team happens to prefer
Who needs to change independently of whom
Whichever line requires the fewest files to move
items.explanation: The unit's guiding rule is that boundaries follow independence of change, not org structure or technology choice — a boundary drawn around the wrong thing just moves the coupling problem somewhere else instead of solving it.
items.reference: Boundary lines follow: who needs to change independently of whom — not org chart, not tech stack.

items.prompt: Two teams sit in the same org unit and report to the same manager, but one owns the mobile experience and the other owns partner integrations, with genuinely different release cadences and consumer needs. Should they share one BFF because they're organizationally close?
choices: Yes — org proximity should always determine service boundaries
Not necessarily — the deciding factor is whether their consumer needs and release cadences genuinely diverge, not where they sit on the org chart
Yes, because sharing a BFF is always cheaper regardless of consumer needs
No decision is needed — every team must always have its own BFF
items.explanation: Org proximity doesn't determine whether a boundary is needed — divergent consumer needs and release cadences do. Two org-adjacent teams with genuinely different needs still benefit from separate BFFs; two org-distant teams with identical needs might not need separate ones at all.
items.reference: Boundary lines follow: who needs to change independently of whom — not org chart, not tech stack.

items.prompt: A team adds a BFF layer but never writes down an explicit contract for what each BFF promises to return. Does the BFF alone stop a breaking change from reaching a consumer?
choices: Yes — a BFF automatically prevents any breaking change
No — a BFF only isolates where consumer-specific logic lives; an explicit contract is what actually stops a breaking change from reaching a consumer
No, and there's no additional step that would help
Yes, but only for internal consumers, never external ones
items.explanation: A BFF changes where consumer-specific logic lives, which limits blast radius, but nothing stops someone from editing that BFF's own response shape carelessly unless there's an explicit, versioned contract governing it — that's a separate discipline layered on top.
items.reference: A BFF decides WHERE a contract is enforced. An explicit, versioned contract is what actually protects a consumer from a breaking change.

items.prompt: Why does the partner's contract need to be more strictly versioned than an internal mobile app's contract, according to L2?
choices: Partners are always less technically competent than internal teams
An external, slow-to-update consumer like a partner usually can't be redeployed on your schedule, so breaking their contract hurts for months instead of minutes
There's no actual difference — all consumers should be treated identically
Partner contracts are legally required to be versioned, internal ones are not
items.explanation: The deciding factor is deploy control: an internal consumer can often be fixed and redeployed quickly, while an external partner's integration may take weeks or months to update — so a breaking change to their contract has a much longer-lived blast radius.
items.reference: A BFF decides WHERE a contract is enforced. An explicit, versioned contract is what actually protects a consumer from a breaking change.

items.prompt: Is it accurate to say a mature architecture must choose between an API gateway and BFFs, but never use both?
choices: Yes — a gateway and BFFs are mutually exclusive alternatives
No — a mature setup often has both: the gateway handles cross-cutting concerns in front, and BFFs behind it handle per-consumer shaping
Yes, because gateways already do everything a BFF does
No, because BFFs replace the need for a gateway entirely
items.explanation: A gateway and BFFs solve different problems and compose naturally — the gateway sits in front handling auth/rate-limiting/routing for all traffic, while BFFs sit behind it shaping responses per consumer type.
items.reference: Gateway (cross-cutting, in front) + BFFs (per-consumer shaping, behind it) — often used together, not as alternatives.

items.prompt: In the worked example, `CoreProduct` holds fields like `promotion` and `relatedProductIds` with no web/mobile/partner-specific naming or shaping. Why is it written this way instead of directly matching one consumer's needs?
choices: It's an arbitrary style choice with no real reason
Because the core service is meant to describe what a product IS to the business, and stay the single source of truth every BFF shapes independently from
Because TypeScript requires all interfaces to be consumer-agnostic
Because it needs to match the partner's contract exactly
items.explanation: The core service is deliberately free of any single consumer's opinions — that's what lets every BFF (web, mobile, partner) shape it differently without any of them fighting over the shared type's shape.
items.reference:
interface CoreProduct {
  id: string; name: string;
  priceCents: number; ...
}

Why: one neutral core type, shaped differently by each BFF.

items.prompt: `web-bff.ts` defines its own `promoBadge` field, computed from `core.promotion?.label`. Why doesn't `promoBadge` just get added directly to `CoreProduct` instead?
choices: TypeScript doesn't allow optional fields on shared interfaces
Because `promoBadge` is a web-only, presentation-specific concept — adding it to the shared core type would leak a web concern into every other consumer's dependency
It would be added to CoreProduct, but the example made a mistake
Because promoBadge is a required field for all consumers
items.explanation: `promoBadge` exists specifically for the web homepage banner — a presentation concern, not a fact about the product. Keeping it inside `web-bff.ts` means renaming or removing it can never affect mobile or the partner, since neither imports from that file.
items.reference:
interface CoreProduct {
  id: string; name: string;
  priceCents: number; ...
}

Why: one neutral core type, shaped differently by each BFF.

items.prompt: Write `shapeMobileProduct(core)` that takes an object with `id`, `name`, `priceCents`, and `averageRating` fields and returns a lean object with only `id`, `name`, `priceCents`, and `rating` (the average rating rounded to 1 decimal place). This mirrors `mobile-bff.ts`'s job: shape the shared core data into exactly what one consumer needs, nothing more.

tests.description: returns only the four lean fields

tests.expr: expect(shapeMobileProduct({ id: 'sku-1', name: 'Mug', priceCents: 1299, averageRating: 3.0 })).toEqual({ id: 'sku-1', name: 'Mug', priceCents: 1299, rating: 3 })

items.explanation: This is the whole idea of a BFF in miniature: take the shared core shape and return only what this one consumer needs, computed independently of any other consumer's shaping logic. Nothing here can affect a differently-shaped web or partner response, because neither reads this function.
items.reference:
A BFF's job: take the shared core data, return only what THIS consumer needs.

Why: shaping logic scoped to one consumer can never leak into another's response.

items.prompt: Write `isBreakingFieldChange(oldFields, newFields)` that takes two arrays of field names representing a contract's old and new shape, and returns `true` if the change is breaking — meaning any field present in `oldFields` is missing from `newFields` (a removal or rename). Adding new fields should NOT count as breaking.

tests.description: renaming a field (old name missing) is breaking
adding a new field only is not breaking

items.explanation: The definition used throughout this unit: a change is breaking specifically when something a consumer already relies on disappears or changes meaning — not when something new is added that old consumers can simply ignore. This function encodes exactly that asymmetry.
items.reference: Breaking = something already relied on disappears or changes. Adding new fields is not breaking.

items.prompt: Write `getPartnerPrice(product, version)` that takes a product object `{ id, name, priceCents }` and a version string. For `'v1'` it should return the price in dollars as `priceUsd` (priceCents / 100). For `'v2'` it should return the price in cents as `priceCents`, unchanged. This mirrors `partner-api.ts`: both versions read the same underlying data but expose a different, frozen shape.

tests.description: v1 for a whole-dollar price has no floating point noise

items.explanation: Both versions read the exact same underlying priceCents value, but each returns a permanently frozen shape for its own consumers. v1's priceUsd field never changes meaning once published — a pricing model change becomes v3, not a silent edit to v1.
items.reference: v1 and v2 both read the same data, but each version's shape is frozen once published.

items.prompt: Write `checkPartnerV1Contract(product)` that throws an `Error` with a message describing the first missing field if `product` is missing any of `productId`, `displayName`, or `priceUsd`. If all three are present, it should return `true`. This mirrors the consumer-driven contract test from L3: it encodes what the partner's v1 integration actually depends on, so an accidental field rename fails loudly instead of shipping silently.

tests.description: passes when all three fields are present
throws when priceUsd is missing (renamed to priceCents)

items.explanation: This is exactly the missing evidence from L3's opening scenario: a test that fails specifically when a field the partner depends on disappears, regardless of whether the web team's own tests still pass. Without something like this checked into CI, a rename can merge cleanly and only break in production.
items.reference: A consumer-driven contract test encodes what the CONSUMER needs, not what the implementer's own tests happen to cover.

items.prompt: Write `mergeNonBreaking(base, additions)` that returns a new object combining `base` with `additions`, but throws an `Error` if any key in `additions` already exists in `base` with a different value (that would be a silent overwrite of an existing field — a breaking change in disguise). If a key in `additions` matches an existing key with the SAME value, that's fine, just keep it.

tests.expr: expect(mergeNonBreaking({ id: 'a' }, { onSale: true })).toEqual({ id: 'a', onSale: true })

tests.description: allows re-setting an existing key to the same value
tests.expr: expect(mergeNonBreaking({ id: 'a', onSale: true }, { onSale: true })).toEqual({ id: 'a', onSale: true })

tests.description: throws when trying to silently overwrite an existing field with a different value

items.explanation: This encodes the non-breaking-change definition from L2 in code: genuinely new fields merge freely, but changing the value of a field a consumer might already depend on is treated as an error rather than silently accepted — the same discipline a real schema-diffing tool in CI would enforce.
items.reference: Non-breaking = adding new fields. Changing an existing field's value is breaking, even via a 'merge'.

items.prompt: A future change removes the `description` field entirely from `CoreProduct`. Does the BFF layer, on its own, protect `mobile-bff.ts` from this change, given that `mobile-bff.ts` never reads `description`?
choices: Yes, completely — mobile-bff.ts is fully isolated from any change to CoreProduct
No — every BFF still imports and depends directly on CoreProduct's actual shape, so a change to the shared core type is a different risk than a change to another BFF's consumer-specific fields
Yes, but only because TypeScript makes all fields optional by default
This scenario cannot happen if BFFs are used correctly
items.explanation: The BFF pattern isolates consumers from each other's consumer-specific shaping, not from the shared core type underneath all of them. Every BFF still compiles against the same CoreProduct interface — which is exactly why the core service's own contract needs explicit versioning discipline too, not just a BFF layer on top of it.
items.reference: BFFs isolate consumer-specific fields from each other. They do NOT version-protect the shared core type underneath them — that needs its own discipline.

items.prompt: What is the actual limit of the BFF pattern that L3 calls out explicitly?
choices: BFFs make deploys slower with no other trade-off
BFFs isolate consumer-specific shaping from each other, but every BFF still depends directly on the shared core service's own shape — so the core contract needs its own versioning discipline
BFFs cannot be written in TypeScript
BFFs eliminate the need for any contract tests
items.explanation: A BFF's isolation stops at the boundary between consumer-specific fields — the shared core service underneath every BFF is still a real, shared dependency, which is why L3 layers explicit versioning (Step 3) and consumer-driven contract tests (Step 4) on top of the BFF split, rather than treating BFFs alone as sufficient.
items.reference: BFFs isolate consumer-specific fields from each other. They do NOT version-protect the shared core type underneath them — that needs its own discipline.

items.prompt: The opening scenario's PR renames a field directly on a shared endpoint, and every test in the repository passes. Why couldn't any of those tests catch the problem?
choices: The tests were poorly written by an inexperienced engineer
Every test in the repository was written by the web team against the web team's own usage — none of them encoded what the mobile app or the partner actually depended on
The testing framework used doesn't support renamed fields
The tests could have caught it, but were skipped in CI
items.explanation: Green CI only proves the tests that exist pass — it says nothing about consumers with no representation in the test suite. Without a test standing in for the partner's or mobile's actual expectations, a rename that only affects them has no way to turn CI red.
items.reference: Green CI means "the tests that ran passed" — not "nothing broke." A consumer with no test has no voice in CI.

items.prompt: What specifically would a consumer-driven contract test for the partner's v1 API have added, that the web team's own test suite did not have?
choices: Faster test execution time
A test encoding the partner's actual expected field names and types, independent of whatever the web team happened to test for their own usage
A way to skip testing entirely for external consumers
Automatic renaming of fields to keep everyone in sync
items.explanation: A consumer-driven contract test represents the consumer's real, published expectations as its own artifact — decoupled from whatever the implementing team's own tests happen to cover — so a change that only breaks that consumer still fails CI instead of merging silently.
items.reference: Green CI means "the tests that ran passed" — not "nothing broke." A consumer with no test has no voice in CI.

items.prompt: According to L3's closing section, when should a team NOT add a BFF, gateway, or micro-frontend split?
choices: Never — every backend should have all three patterns applied by default
When there is only one real consumer and no genuinely diverging needs to isolate, since the boundary's coordination cost buys nothing in that case
Only when the team is too small to maintain extra services, regardless of consumer count
Only for internal tools, but always for anything partner-facing
items.explanation: The deciding factor is the same one used throughout the unit: boundaries exist to isolate consumers with diverging needs from each other. With a single consumer, there's no second party to isolate from, so the extra service is pure coordination cost with no benefit.
items.reference: A boundary added where there's only one real consumer is coordination cost with nothing bought in return.

items.prompt: A single internal admin tool has exactly one consumer (the ops team) and will likely stay that way. A reviewer suggests splitting it behind a BFF 'to future-proof it.' What does L3's closing argument say about this suggestion?
choices: It's a good default — always add a BFF regardless of current consumer count
It's premature — a boundary should be added when consumers' needs genuinely diverge or need independent deploys, not as a speculative default architecture
It's required by this unit's rules for every backend service
It only matters if the admin tool is written in TypeScript
items.explanation: L3 explicitly argues against defaulting to boundary patterns — they should be added in response to genuinely diverging consumer needs or deploy independence requirements, not speculatively 'just in case' a second consumer someday appears.
items.reference: A boundary added where there's only one real consumer is coordination cost with nothing bought in return.
